opus-5.5.text:
I think the single most important thing is just to build things, and to build them in a way where you actually hit real problems. A lot of people approach this by reading papers or taking courses, and those are useful for getting a foundation, but the engineering skill really comes from sitting down with a codebase and trying to make something work, then debugging it when it doesn't, which is most of the time.

For AI engineering specifically, I'd suggest picking a project that's a bit beyond your current ability. Something like implementing a transformer from scratch and training it on a small dataset, or trying to reproduce a result from a paper. When you do that, you run into all the stuff that the paper doesn't tell you: your loss is going to NaN and you don't know why, your training is way slower than it should be, you've got a subtle bug in your attention masking that makes everything look almost right. Learning to track those things down is a huge part of the job.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that a lot of the work at a place like Anthropic is less about clever ML ideas and more about solid software engineering at scale. Can you write code that other people can read and build on? Can you profile something and figure out where the bottleneck is? Do you understand how things work across many GPUs, how communication works, what's going on with memory? Those skills transfer from general software engineering, so if you've got a background there, it's more applicable than people sometimes think.

And then I'd say work with people who are better than you if you can. Getting code review from someone really strong, or pair programming with them, teaches you a ton that's hard to pick up alone: how they approach a problem, what they check first, what shortcuts they take and which ones they refuse to take.

Finally, don't wait until you feel "ready." People often think they need to finish some long list of prerequisites before they can contribute, but in practice you learn fastest by jumping in on real problems and filling in the gaps as you go.

r002.rationale: It recommends code review or pairing with a strong engineer, but does not identify contributing to open source or mentorship from project maintainers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I'd say is that it's much more about practice than about studying. A lot of people think they need to go read a bunch of papers or take a bunch of courses first, and I actually think that's mostly not the right approach. The way you get good at engineering is by writing a lot of code, running into problems, and fixing them.

So concretely, what I'd recommend is picking a project that's a bit beyond what you currently know how to do, and then just building it. For ML specifically, a really good one is implementing something like a small transformer from scratch, training it on some dataset, and getting it to actually work. Not just copying the code from a tutorial, but trying to do it yourself, getting stuck, debugging it, and figuring out why your loss isn't going down. That debugging process is honestly most of the job. When I'm working on training runs at Anthropic, a huge fraction of the time is spent on things like, "Why is this slower than it should be?" or "Why did this number come out wrong?" And the skill of carefully narrowing down where the problem is, forming hypotheses and testing them, is something you really only learn by doing it a lot.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the skills are just regular software engineering skills. Writing clean code, understanding how to profile things, knowing how your code actually runs on the hardware, being comfortable with distributed systems. The ML-specific knowledge you need is honestly smaller than people expect, and you can pick it up fairly quickly once you have a strong engineering base. So if you're coming from a software engineering background, I wouldn't feel like you need to go back and do a PhD or anything like that. You're probably closer than you think.

And then I'd try to get feedback as fast as possible. Working with people who are better than you is the fastest way to improve. So if you can get a job somewhere doing this, even if it's not your dream role, that's often better than spending a year preparing on your own. You'll learn more in a few months of working on real problems with experienced people than you would in a long time studying alone.

r003.rationale: It does not describe open-source contributions as publicly inspectable evidence for employers.

astra-6.text:
I’d recommend learning by building things. Pick a project that you’re excited about, that’s a little beyond what you currently know how to do, and try to get it working end to end. You want something where you can tell whether you’ve succeeded, so you’re getting feedback rather than just reading tutorials and feeling like you understand them.

For AI engineering, that could mean taking an existing model and building an application around it, or implementing a small model and training it yourself. Those teach somewhat different skills. In either case, spend time understanding what’s going wrong: how would you measure performance, what are the failure cases, and what experiment would help you choose the next improvement?

And, if you can, work with people who are better engineers than you. Having someone review your code and explain how they’d approach the problem can accelerate your learning a lot. Courses can help fill gaps, but I’d make the project the central thing, and use the courses and reading to help you get unstuck.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d recommend building things. Pick a project that’s a little beyond what you already know how to do, get something working end to end, and then make it better. You want practice with the whole process: figuring out what to build, debugging it, testing whether it actually works, and making the code understandable enough that someone else can contribute.

For AI engineering specifically, it’s useful to implement a small model and train it yourself. Work through the data pipeline, the training loop, and the evaluations. When something goes wrong, try to understand why. You can learn a lot more from investigating a model that isn’t learning than from following a tutorial where everything works immediately.

And get feedback from good engineers if you can. Working on a team or contributing to an existing project helps you develop judgment about how to structure things and which problems are worth spending time on. You don’t need every project to be novel; the point is to take increasing responsibility for getting something real to work.
